Ganeshalingam, <email>ashok.ganeshalingam@rsyd.dk</email></corresp></author-notes><pub-date pub-type="collection"><month>5</month><year>2026</year></pub-date><pub-date pub-type="epub"><day>04</day><month>3</month><year>2026</year></pub-date><volume>49</volume><issue>5</issue><issue-id pub-id-type="pmc-issue-id">512040</issue-id><fpage>800</fpage><lpage>807</lpage><history><date date-type="received" iso-8601-date="2025-09-04"><day>04</day><month>9</month><year>2025</year></date><date date-type="accepted" iso-8601-date="2026-02-01"><day>01</day><month>2</month><year>2026</year></date></history><pub-history><event event-type="pmc-release"><date><day>04</day><month>03</month><year>2026</year></date></event><event event-type="pmc-live"><date><day>21</day><month>04</month><year>2026</year></date></event><event event-type="pmc-last-change"><date iso-8601-date="2026-04-21 16:25:17.410"><day>21</day><month>04</month><year>2026</year></date></event></pub-history><permissions><copyright-statement>© 2026 by the American Diabetes Association</copyright-statement><copyright-year>2026</copyright-year><copyright-holder>American Diabetes Association</copyright-holder><license><ali:license_ref xmlns:ali="http://www.niso.org/schemas/ali/1.0/" start_date="2026-03-04">https://www.diabetesjournals.org/journals/pages/license</ali:license_ref><license-p>Readers may use this work for educational, noncommercial purposes if properly cited and unaltered. This publication and its contents may not be reproduced, distributed, or used for text or data mining, machine learning, or other similar technologies without prior written permission. More information is available at <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:title="Link to Reuse, Licensing, and Public Access" xlink:href="https://diabetesjournals.org/journals/pages/license">https://diabetesjournals.org/journals/pages/license</ext-link>.</license-p></license></permissions><self-uri xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="pmc-pdf" xlink:href="dc252041.pdf"/><self-uri xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="application/pdf" xlink:href="dc252041.pdf"/><abstract><sec><title>OBJECTIVE</title><p>To examine the effects of semaglutide on insulin sensitivity, insulin resistance, and β-cell function and explore whether these changes were mediated by weight loss in overweight or obese individuals with schizophrenia and prediabetes receiving second-generation antipsychotics.</p></sec><sec><title>RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS</title><p>In this 30-week, double-blind trial, 154 participants were randomized to semaglutide (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 77) or placebo (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 77); 141 (91.5%) completed the study. Baseline and end-of-study assessments included fasting glucose, insulin, C-peptide, HOMA2 of β-cell function, HOMA2 of insulin sensitivity, HOMA of insulin resistance, and body weight.</p></sec><sec><title>RESULTS</title><p>Participants (56% women, mean age 38.3 years) provided complete insulin data in 131 cases. Compared with placebo, semaglutide significantly reduced fasting glucose (−0.87 mmol/L [95% CI −1.15, −0.59]; <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> &lt; 0.001), improved insulin sensitivity (8.60 [5.82, 13.65]; <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.001), and lowered insulin resistance (−0.69 [−1.00, −0.20]; <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.006). Mean weight loss was 9.2 kg and mediated improvements in insulin sensitivity (estimate 7.82; <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.01) and insulin resistance (estimate −0.75; <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.01). Nonsignificant trends were observed toward reduced fasting insulin (−52.3 pmol/L; <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.11) and C-peptide (−182.9 pmol/L; <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.096), with a modest, nonsignificant increase in β-cell function (8.10; <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.19).</p></sec><sec><title>CONCLUSIONS</title><p>Semaglutide significantly improved insulin sensitivity, reduced insulin resistance, lowered fasting glucose, and promoted substantial weight loss in patients with antipsychotic-induced metabolic disturbances. Weight loss partly mediated the metabolic improvements, while β-cell function remained largely unchanged. These findings support semaglutide as a potential strategy for mitigating metabolic dysfunction in this high-risk population.</p></sec></abstract><abstract abstract-type="graphical"><title>Graphical Abstract</title><p>
<fig position="float" id="FGA" orientation="portrait"><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="dc252041fGA.jpg"><alt-text>An infographic summarises a 30-week randomised placebo controlled trial of semaglutide 1.0 milligram weekly in patients with schizophrenia, prediabetes, and obesity treated with second-generation antipsychotics. The population includes 154 individuals randomised to Active N 77 or Placebo N 77, with 74 and 69 completing. Main results show fasting glucose decreases by 0.87 millimole per litre, insulin sensitivity increases by 8.60, insulin resistance decreases by 0.69, and weight decreases by 9.2 kilogram. The conclusion states reduced insulin resistance, improved insulin sensitivity, lower fasting glucose, and weight loss.</alt-text></graphic></fig></p></abstract><funding-group><award-group><funding-source>

Health.</funding-statement></funding-group><custom-meta-group><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-status-qastatus</meta-name><meta-value>0</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-status-live</meta-name><meta-value>yes</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-status-embargo</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-status-released</meta-name><meta-value>yes</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-open-access</meta-name><meta-value>yes</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-olf</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-manuscript</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-legally-suppressed</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-has-pdf</meta-name><meta-value>yes</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-has-supplement</meta-name><meta-value>yes</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-pdf-only</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-suppress-copyright</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-is-real-version</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-is-scanned-article</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-preprint</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-in-epmc</meta-name><meta-value>yes</meta-value></custom-meta></custom-meta-group></article-meta></front><body><sec sec-type="intro" id="s1"><title>Introduction</title><p>Individuals with schizophrenia have a significantly shortened life span, with an average reduction of 15–20 years compared with the general population (<xref rid="B1" ref-type="bibr">1</xref>,<xref rid="B2" ref-type="bibr">2</xref>). The increased mortality is largely attributed to a higher prevalence of prediabetes and metabolic syndrome (<xref rid="B3" ref-type="bibr">3</xref>), which elevate the risk of type 2 diabetes (T2D) (<xref rid="B4" ref-type="bibr">4</xref>) and premature cardiovascular disease (CVD) (<xref rid="B5" ref-type="bibr">5</xref>). The metabolic disturbances may stem from the psychiatric condition itself (<xref rid="B6" ref-type="bibr">6</xref>), which negatively impacts the ability to maintain a healthy lifestyle (<xref rid="B7" ref-type="bibr">7</xref>). However, treatment with second-generation antipsychotics (SGAs) (<xref rid="B8" ref-type="bibr">8</xref>) may also play a role, as this group of drugs is documented to promote weight gain and increase appetite shortly after treatment initiation (<xref rid="B9" ref-type="bibr">9</xref>). Insulin resistance is a key metabolic dysfunction that underlies the pathogenesis of obesity, T2D, and hypertension, thereby contributing to an increased cardiovascular mortality (<xref rid="B10" ref-type="bibr">10</xref>). Insulin resistance is characterized by a diminished biological response to insulin in insulin-sensitive tissues, such as muscle, liver, and adipose tissue, leading to glucose intolerance, dyslipidemia, and abnormal protein metabolism (<xref rid="B11" ref-type="bibr">11</xref>). To compensate, pancreatic β-cells increase insulin secretion, often resulting in hyperinsulinemia, which is a hallmark of insulin resistance (<xref rid="B12" ref-type="bibr">12</xref>).</p><p>Over the past decade, various weight loss interventions have been investigated in schizophrenia, including metformin, topiramate, and glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), with the latter demonstrating the most promising results (<xref rid="B13" ref-type="bibr">13</xref>,<xref rid="B14" ref-type="bibr">14</xref>). The initial GLP-1RA–based trials in patients with schizophrenia used either liraglutide or exenatide (<xref rid="B15" ref-type="bibr">15</xref>,<xref rid="B16" ref-type="bibr">16</xref>), but today, semaglutide has largely replaced the early GLP-1RAs due to its superior efficacy in promoting weight loss in individuals with obesity. Additionally, semaglutide has been shown to improve cardiometabolic risk factors and reduce cardiovascular events in individuals with obesity, without diabetes, and with preexisting CVD (<xref rid="B17" ref-type="bibr">17</xref>) and to cause significant weight loss and favorable changes in body composition in individuals with schizophrenia treated with semaglutide 2.0 mg weekly for 36 weeks (<xref rid="B18" ref-type="bibr">18</xref>).</p><p>We recently performed a randomized, 30-week clinical trial that compared up to 1.0 mg weekly of semaglutide with placebo in patients with schizophrenia, overweight/obesity (BMI ≥27 kg/m<sup>2</sup>), and prediabetes (HbA<sub>1c</sub> 39–47 mmol/L) who were on stable treatment with SGAs (<xref rid="B19" ref-type="bibr">19</xref>). Semaglutide treatment was well tolerated and improved patients’ physical well-being without worsening their mental disorder. In addition, semaglutide reduced HbA<sub>1c</sub> by 5.07 mmol/mol, reduced body weight by 9.21 kg, and normalized HbA<sub>1c</sub> to &lt;39 mmol/mol in 81% of semaglutide-treated patients vs. 19% in placebo-treated patients. The objective of this prespecified secondary end point study was to describe in more detail the glucose-metabolic changes in our cohort, focusing on HOMA-derived measures of β-cell function (HOMA-B) and insulin sensitivity (HOMA2-S) and to compare these changes with changes in body weight.</p></sec><sec id="s2"><title>Research Design and Methods</title><p>This trial was approved by the Regional Committees on Health Research Ethics for Southern Denmark, Odense, Denmark (S-20200182), and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. The study was initiated prior to the introduction of Wegovy (semaglutide up to 2.4 mg weekly; Novo Nordisk A/S, Bagsværd, Denmark); therefore, semaglutide was tested up to doses of 1 mg weekly only. As semaglutide 1 mg weekly is not approved for the treatment of patients with schizophrenia, overweight/obesity, and prediabetes, the study protocol received prior approval from the Danish Medicines Agency (2020110216). The trial was subsequently subject to close monitoring by local Good Clinical Practice units.</p><sec id="s2A"><title>Design</title><p>This investigator-initiated, double-blind, parallel-group, superiority, multicenter, randomized controlled trial (RCT) took place from January 2022 (first patient, first visit) to May 2024 (last patient, last visit) in the Region of Southern Denmark and the Region of Zealand, covering all community psychiatry centers. The majority of participants’ blood samples were collected in their homes through Project HISTORI (Home-Based Intervention With Semaglutide Treatment of Neuroleptic-Related Prediabetes).</p><p>This study reports a prespecified secondary end point. A detailed description of the study protocol has been published previously, and additional information about both the primary and secondary end points is available at ClinicalTrials.gov (identifier: <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="pmc:clinical-trial" xlink:href="NCT05193578">NCT05193578</ext-link>) and in the published protocol (<xref rid="B20" ref-type="bibr">20</xref>). The prespecified primary end point was change in HbA<sub>1c</sub>. Other prespecified secondary end points included changes in weight, BMI, cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy, schizophrenia symptom severity, quality of life, physical activity levels, and adherence to antipsychotic treatment.</p></sec><sec id="s2B"><title>Participants</title><p>The study enrolled patients clinically diagnosed with either schizophrenia, schizotypal disorder, or schizoaffective disorder according to ICD-10 codes F20.x, F21.x, and F25.x. All patients were between 18 and 60 years of age and received SGA treatment. Furthermore, all patients had prediabetes (defined as an HbA<sub>1c</sub> of 39–47 mmol/mol) and overweight/obesity (defined by a BMI ≥27 kg/m<sup>2</sup>). A comprehensive list of all relevant inclusion and exclusion criteria can be found in <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://doi.org/10.2337/figshare.31298458" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:title="Link to Semaglutide Effects on Insulin Sensitivity and β-Cell Function in Patients With Schizophrenia, Prediabetes, and Obesity Treated With Second-Generation Antipsychotics: Findings From the HISTORI Trial, a 30-Week Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Trial With Semaglutide 1.0 mg Weekly">Supplementary Table 1</ext-link>. None of the participants in the study received any compensation, aside from mileage allowances, for participation.</p></sec><sec id="s2C"><title>Procedures</title><p>Participants received semaglutide (1.34 mg/mL) up to 1.0 mg/week or a similar volume of placebo for 30 weeks with injection once weekly. Semaglutide and placebo were uptitrated according to recommendations by the manufacturer (Novo Nordisk). Novo Nordisk provided the study drug (active comparator and placebo) and randomization list but was not involved in the study.</p><p>At baseline and at 30 weeks of treatment, all participants gave fasting blood samples for assessments of HbA<sub>1c</sub>, triglycerides, cholesterol (HDL and LDL), fasting blood glucose, insulin, and C-peptide. We also registered their BMI, waist circumference, and blood pressure.</p><p>The outcomes were changes in HOMA2 estimates, calculated using HOMA2 (version 2.2.3) based on fasting blood glucose and fasting insulin levels. Samples were analyzed at the Department of Biochemistry, Odense University Hospital, according to International Federation of Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine standards. All the samples were measured en bloc after finalizing the last patient, last visit. Other variables, such as HbA<sub>1c</sub> and lipid levels, were measured at the department of biochemistry at local hospitals after ensuring that they used the same assays and platforms. All patients followed their clinical psychiatric treatment plan, with individually adjusted follow-up visits at their usual clinician/treatment facility independent of the study.</p></sec><sec id="s2D"><title>Randomization and Blinding</title><p>Block randomization (blocks of four or six participants) was used. The randomization list was provided by Novo Nordisk. Participants were assigned a randomization number upon study entry using Research Electronic Data Capture, and randomization was conducted continuously without stratification. Each number corresponded to a prepackaged set of study medication or placebo for the entire study period.</p><p>All participants and study personnel were blinded; only the pharmacy had access to the randomization list. The trial drug and placebo were visually identical, medication packs were labeled with participant numbers, and unblinded pharmacy staff had no contact with blinded investigators. Unblinding occurred only after all end points were assessed, except for one participant who died of natural causes and was later revealed to have received placebo.</p></sec><sec id="s2E"><title>Variables of Interest and Interpretation</title><sec id="s2E1"><title>β-Cell Function</title><p>β-Cell function was estimated using the HOMA-B, which is a widely used method to estimate pancreatic β-cell function based on fasting glucose and insulin levels. This model assumes a steady-state relationship between insulin secretion and glucose levels, providing an indirect measure of β-cell activity. HOMA-B is particularly useful due to its simplicity, but it has limitations, especially in individuals with extreme glucose levels, where its accuracy may be reduced. Despite these constraints, HOMA-B remains a valuable tool for assessing β-cell function in both research and clinical settings (<xref rid="B21" ref-type="bibr">21</xref>).</p></sec><sec id="s2E2"><title>Insulin Sensitivity</title><p>Insulin sensitivity refers to how effectively the tissues, particularly muscle, liver, and fat cells, respond to insulin and take up glucose from the blood stream. Insulin sensitivity may be estimated by HOMA-S. HOMA-S aligns with the gold standard of the euglycemic-hyperinsulinemic clamp, making the model useful in clinical settings (<xref rid="B22" ref-type="bibr">22</xref>).</p></sec></sec><sec id="s2F"><title>Statistical Analysis</title><p>The power calculation was based on HbA<sub>1c</sub> changes. Assuming that 30 weeks of semaglutide would reduce HbA<sub>1c</sub> by 0.2% and an SD of 0.35%, 65 participants in each arm were required to obtain a power of 90% with a two-sided significance level of 5%. This study was not powered to detect changes in insulin-related end points.</p><p>To assess sample reproducibility and treatment group exchangeability, we conducted descriptive analyses. Categorical outcomes are reported as numbers and percentages and analyzed using Fisher exact test or χ<sup>2</sup> test. Continuous outcomes are described as mean (SD) or median (interquartile range) and analyzed using the Wilcoxon rank sum test or unpaired <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> test.</p><p>HOMA outcomes were analyzed using a mixed-effects model, which was preferred over G-computation due to the absence of time-varying exposure and confounding. A likelihood ratio test was used to assess the longitudinal effect of semaglutide. Treatment effects at weeks 15 and 30 were tested via mixed-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood estimation and a <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> test using the Kenward-Roger method. Models included baseline covariates and time interactions, with fit assessed via normality of residuals and random effects; bootstrapping was applied if needed. The discrimination between high and low insulin sensitivity (HOMA2-S) and β-cell function (HOMA2-B) was defined by the median of HOMA2-B = 115.3 and HOMA2-S = 63.5 in a matched background population with normal glucose tolerance (<xref rid="B23" ref-type="bibr">23</xref>).</p><p>Mediator analysis among the exposure, treatment assignment, mediator, weight loss, and outcome followed a counterfactual framework, adjusting for baseline by evaluating changes over time and thereafter analyzed in a cross-sectional manner. Therefore, we used G-computation, in which the Q-model was chosen to be a linear regression at each time point. The statistical tests for the three effects (natural direct, indirect, and total effect) were based on a <italic toggle="yes">z</italic> test. The CIs for the effects were constructed such that they realigned with the <italic toggle="yes">z</italic> test with robust SEs. The model assumptions for the three Q-models were checked via quantile-quantile plots. For the three models, none of them were adjusted for potential confounders except the models focusing on the association between the mediator and outcome, which were adjusted for sex.</p><p>Efficacy and safety were analyzed using an intention-to-treat approach, in which participants who received at least one dose and had postbaseline assessments where analyzed according to the assigned group. Safety analysis included all randomized participants who received at least one dose. Treatment groups were unblinded after the statistical analyses.</p><p>Statistical analyses were performed using Stata 18 (StataCorp, College Station, TX). Two-sided <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> values and 95% CIs are reported, with an α of 0.05. No multiple-testing adjustments were made, as analyses were prespecified.</p></sec></sec><sec sec-type="results" id="s3"><title>Results</title><p>We assessed 402 potential participants for eligibility, of whom 154 were randomized to 77 in each arm (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://doi.org/10.2337/figshare.31298458" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:title="Link to Semaglutide Effects on Insulin Sensitivity and β-Cell Function in Patients With Schizophrenia, Prediabetes, and Obesity Treated With Second-Generation Antipsychotics: Findings From the HISTORI Trial, a 30-Week Randomized, Place">Supplementary Fig. 1</ext-link>). A total of 141 participants (91.5%) completed the trial (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://doi.org/10.2337/figshare.31298458" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:title="Link to Semaglutide Effects on Insulin Sensitivity and β-Cell Function in Patients With Schizophrenia, Prediabetes, and Obesity Treated With Second-Generation Antipsychotics: Findings From the HISTORI Trial, a 30-Week Randomized, Place">Supplementary Fig. 1</ext-link>), including 74 (96%) randomized to semaglutide and 67 randomized to placebo (87%). The randomization resulted in two comparable groups (<xref rid="T1" ref-type="table">Table 1</xref>). The original publication provides additional information on the study groups (<xref rid="B19" ref-type="bibr">19</xref>).</p><table-wrap position="float" id="T1" orientation="portrait"><label>Table 1</label><caption><p>Baseline characteristics of study participants</p></caption><alt-text>A table presents baseline characteristics for Active, n 77, and Placebo, n 77, groups with P values. Per protocol, all participants had prediabetes according to HbA<sub>1c</sub>.</p><p>Baseline levels of fasting C-peptide, fasting insulin, and fasting glucose were comparable between the groups (<xref rid="T1" ref-type="table">Table 1</xref>). Compared with placebo, semaglutide tended to reduce C-peptide (−182.93 pmol/L [95% CI, −260.36, 32.19]; <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.096) and tended to improve insulin (−52.30 pmol/L [−74.40, 11.61]; <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.11), whereas fasting plasma glucose was significantly lower (−0.87 mmol/L [−1.15, 0.59]; <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> &lt; 0.001) (<xref rid="T2" ref-type="table">Table 2</xref>).</p><table-wrap position="float" id="T2" orientation="portrait"><label>Table 2</label><caption><p>Main effects on outcomes</p></caption><alt-text>A table presents outcomes for Semaglutide, active comparator, and Placebo with treatment effect or difference and P values. Significant differences favour semaglutide for weight, waist circumference, body mass index, H b A 1 c, fasting blood glucose, insulin sensitivity, and insulin resistance.</alt-text><table frame="hsides" rules="groups"><thead><tr><th id="t2c1" scope="col" align="left" rowspan="1" colspan="1">Outcome</th><th id="t2c2" scope="col" align="center" rowspan="1" colspan="1">Semaglutide (active comparator)</th><th id="t2c3" scope="col" align="center" rowspan="1" colspan="1">Placebo</th><th id="t2c4" scope="col" align="center" rowspan="1" colspan="1">Treatment effect/difference</th><th id="t2c5" scope="col" align="center" rowspan="1" colspan="1">

BP, blood pressure; FBG, fasting blood glucose. Some data are reprinted from our initial study (19).</p></fn></table-wrap-foot></table-wrap><p>At baseline, HOMA estimates showed comparable β-cell function and insulin sensitivity in the two groups (<xref rid="F1" ref-type="fig">Fig. 1</xref>). After 30 weeks, β-cell function had increased numerically in the semaglutide group (8.00 [95% CI, −1.66, 17.65]) and remained unchanged in the placebo group (−0.10 [−8.54, 8.33]), but overall, semaglutide caused a nonsignificant increase in β-cell function (8.10 [−1.66, 20.22]; <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.19) (<xref rid="T2" ref-type="table">Table 2</xref>). In contrast, insulin sensitivity increased significantly in the semaglutide-treated group (10.08 [5.82, 14.33]) compared with the placebo-treated group (1.48 [−2.79, 5.75]), resulting in a significant treatment effect averaging 8.60 (5.82, 13.65; <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.001) (<xref rid="F1" ref-type="fig">Fig. 1</xref>).</p><fig position="float" id="F1" orientation="portrait"><label>Figure 1</label><caption><p>Margin plots of HOMA2-B and HOMA2-S. <italic toggle="yes">A</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">B</italic>: HOMA2 estimates of insulin sensitivity (<italic toggle="yes">A</italic>) and β-cell function (<italic toggle="yes">B</italic>) at baseline and week 30 for participants receiving semaglutide or placebo. At week 30, semaglutide significantly increased insulin sensitivity (mean difference 8.60 [95% CI 5.82, 13.65]; <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.001). β-Cell function showed a modest, nonsignificant improvement (mean difference 8.60 [–2.53, 19.73]; <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.13). Data are mean ± SE.</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="dc252041f1.jpg"><alt-text>Two line charts labelled A and B show insulin sensitivity and beta cell function using H O M A percent S and H O M A percent B at Baseline and week 30. In A, the Active group rises from about 35 at Baseline to about 45 at week 30, while the Placebo group rises slightly from about 35 to about 37. In B, the Active group rises from about 157 at Baseline to about 165 at week 30, while the Placebo group remains near 157. Error bars appear at each point.</alt-text></graphic></fig><p>To contextualize our findings, we compared our study cohort with previously published data from our institution on individuals with normal glucose tolerance (<xref rid="B23" ref-type="bibr">23</xref>), illustrating insulin sensitivity and β-cell function using a two-dimensional distribution (<xref rid="F2" ref-type="fig">Fig. 2</xref>). The majority of participants showed increased β-cell function and reduced insulin sensitivity, indicating an elevated insulin resistance.</p><fig position="float" id="F2" orientation="portrait"><label>Figure 2</label><caption><p>Baseline association between HOMA-S and HOMA-B. Plot of insulin sensitivity and β-cell function of patients at baseline. Reference lines represent the median values of HOMA2-S and HOMA2-B in the background population. Red circles indicate insulinopenic phenotype; dark blue circles, classical phenotype; light blue circles, hyperinsulinemic phenotype.</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="dc252041f2.jpg"><alt-text>A scatter plot shows H O M A 2 percent B on the vertical axis and H O M A 2 percent S on the horizontal axis. The data points cluster at lower percent S values between about 10 and 50, with percent B ranging from about 80 to 300. Fewer points appear above 60 percent S, where percent B is mostly below 120. A vertical line marks about 63.5 on percent S, and a horizontal line marks about 115.3 on percent B.</alt-text></graphic></fig><sec id="s3A"><title>Weight Loss and HOMA Values</title><p>Mediator analysis indicated that weight loss significantly mediated the effect of semaglutide on improving insulin sensitivity (estimate 7.82 [95% CI 1.83, 13.81]; <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.01). In contrast, weight loss was not a significant mediator for changes in fasting C-peptide (estimate −190.47 [−440.75, 59.81]; <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.14), changes in fasting insulin (estimate −61.13 [−146.30, 24.03]; <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.16), or the increase in β-cell function (estimate 9.31 [−5.21, 23.82]; <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = 0.21) (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://doi.org/10.2337/figshare.31298458" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:title="Link to Semaglutide Effects on Insulin Sensitivity and β-Cell Function in Patients With Schizophrenia, Prediabetes, and Obesity Treated With Second-Generation Antipsychotics: Findings From the HISTORI Trial, a 30-Week Randomized, Place">Supplementary Table 2</ext-link>).</p></sec><sec id="s3B"><title>Antipsychotic Treatment and HOMA Values</title><p>There were no associations between the type of antipsychotic treatment and pretreatment HOMA estimates of β-cell function or insulin sensitivity (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://doi.org/10.2337/figshare.31298458" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:title="Link to Semaglutide Effects on Insulin Sensitivity and β-Cell Function in Patients With Schizophrenia, Prediabetes, and Obesity Treated With Second-Generation Antipsychotics: Findings From the HISTORI Trial, a 30-Week Randomized, Place">Supplementary Tables 3</ext-link> and <xref rid="B4" ref-type="bibr">4</xref> and <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://doi.org/10.2337/figshare.31298458" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:title="Link to Semaglutide Effects on Insulin Sensitivity and β-Cell Function in Patients With Schizophrenia, Prediabetes, and Obesity Treated With Second-Generation Antipsychotics: Findings From the HISTORI Trial, a 30-Week Randomized, Place">Supplementary Fig. 2</ext-link>).</p></sec></sec><sec sec-type="conclusion" id="s4"><title>Conclusions</title><p>In this article, we describe changes in β-cell function and insulin sensitivity in individuals with SGA-treated schizophrenia, prediabetes, and overweight/obesity. These data are based on our recently performed double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT, in which we compared 30 weeks of semaglutide up to 1.0 mg weekly versus placebo. We could demonstrate that semaglutide was well-tolerated, reduced mean body weight by 9.2 kg (∼7.5% of the body weight), and reduced HbA<sub>1c</sub> to 5.07 mmol/mol, alongside an improvement in physical quality of life, compared with placebo (<xref rid="B19" ref-type="bibr">19</xref>). We were also able to demonstrate that the semaglutide-treated group, alongside the reduction in HbA<sub>1c</sub>, showed improvements in fasting blood glucose, while its effects on fasting C-peptide and insulin levels did not reach statistical significance. Here, we describe changes in glucose homeostasis in further detail by demonstrating that insulin sensitivity/resistance improved significantly with semaglutide treatment, whereas β-cell function remained unchanged, and that the semaglutide-induced weight loss was the mediator of the beneficial changes in insulin sensitivity/resistance.</p><sec id="s4A"><title>Hyperinsulinemia, Insulin Sensitivity, and β-Cell Function</title><p>Using HOMA2 estimates, we demonstrated that at baseline, our participants had reduced insulin sensitivity and elevated β-cell function compared with individuals without diabetes and schizophrenia (<xref rid="F2" ref-type="fig">Fig. 2</xref>). Even though the participants in our trial had prediabetes and not overt T2D, the majority exhibited insulin levels similar to individuals with T2D and highest levels of insulin resistance (<xref rid="B23" ref-type="bibr">23</xref>). Furthermore, our data align well with a meta-analysis performed by Pillinger et al. (<xref rid="B6" ref-type="bibr">6</xref>), who showed that individuals with schizophrenia exhibit elevated fasting plasma glucose levels, diminished glucose tolerance, increased fasting plasma insulin levels, and enhanced insulin resistance at the onset of illness.</p><p>After 30 weeks, semaglutide treatment could be linked to a significant increase in insulin sensitivity and a corresponding decrease in insulin resistance. This finding suggests that the semaglutide-induced improvement in glucose regulation is driven, at least in part, by enhanced insulin action rather than direct effects on β-cell function.</p><p>Despite improvements in glucose metabolism (HbA<sub>1c</sub> and fasting glucose), as well as insulin sensitivity, β-cell function, as assessed by HOMA-B, remained unchanged following semaglutide treatment. While GLP-1RAs have been shown to enhance β-cell function in some studies (<xref rid="B24" ref-type="bibr">24</xref>,<xref rid="B25" ref-type="bibr">25</xref>), the current findings suggest that in our population, the primary driver of metabolic improvements was weight loss rather than direct β-cell effects.</p><p>The mediator analyses suggest that the beneficial effects of semaglutide on glucose metabolism and insulin homeostasis are largely mediated by semaglutide’s weight-reducing properties rather than direct pharmacological effects on insulin secretion or β-cell function. Thus, our findings align with evidence derived from the Semaglutide Treatment Effect in People With Obesity (STEP) and Semaglutide Effects on Cardiovascular Outcomes in People With Overweight and Obesity (SELECT) programs and with mediation analyses showing that GLP-1RA–associated improvements in glycemia, lipid parameters, and CVD risk are mediated by weight loss (<xref rid="B26" ref-type="bibr">26</xref>). It is important to note that semaglutide 1.0 mg weekly for 30 weeks was used in this trial. Studies using semaglutide 2.4 mg have shown an average weight loss of 15% following 68 weeks treatment (<xref rid="B27" ref-type="bibr">27</xref>). Using semaglutide 2.4 mg over a longer duration might have had a greater effect on glucose metabolism and insulin homeostasis.</p><p>Insulin resistance has been linked to an increased risk for CVD (<xref rid="B28" ref-type="bibr">28</xref>,<xref rid="B29" ref-type="bibr">29</xref>). As weight loss appeared to mediate the observed beneficial effects of semaglutide on insulin sensitivity/resistance, our findings suggest that the treatment of patients with schizoaffective disorder should include weight loss to prevent CVD (<xref rid="B30" ref-type="bibr">30</xref>).</p></sec><sec id="s4B"><title>Antipsychotic Treatment and Metabolic Outcomes</title><p>Antipsychotic medications, which are fundamental in the treatment of severe mental illnesses such as schizophrenia spectrum disorders, substantially elevate the risk of metabolic complications. These adverse effects include weight gain, dyslipidemia, and insulin resistance (<xref rid="B3" ref-type="bibr">3</xref>,<xref rid="B31" ref-type="bibr">31</xref>). As evidenced by an extensive Danish cohort study, all types of antipsychotics increase the risk of T2D, regardless of the specific agent or class, whether first or second generation (<xref rid="B8" ref-type="bibr">8</xref>). This notion aligns with our data, as we did not detect any correlation between specific antipsychotic drugs and HOMA values. Although treatment with clozapine and olanzapine has been associated with increases in plasma glucose (<xref rid="B32" ref-type="bibr">32</xref>), we did not observe any specific correlation between treatment with these drugs and the HOMA estimates. However, we acknowledge that our sample size was small and that only 22 of 154 participants received olanzapine and only 41 of 154 received clozapine. Thus, the comparison of different SGAs remains of an explorative nature, as the study was not powered to evaluate antipsychotic effects on insulin sensitivity or β-cell function.</p><p>Metabolic syndrome in patients with schizophrenia is partly driven by antipsychotics, causing increased appetite, weight gain, and consequently, insulin resistance and abdominal obesity (<xref rid="B33" ref-type="bibr">33</xref>). Insulin resistance can lead to T2D, dyslipidemia, and essential hypertension (<xref rid="B34" ref-type="bibr">34</xref>), which are key contributors to atherosclerosis. Consequently, the increased CVD mortality in patients with schizophrenia may be explained by the increased prevalence and severity of insulin resistance (<xref rid="B5" ref-type="bibr">5</xref>). The most effective way to treat insulin resistance is through weight loss, which reduces abdominal fat (<xref rid="B35" ref-type="bibr">35</xref>). Caloric restriction and increased physical activity are crucial, and there is evidence that they can reverse insulin resistance (<xref rid="B36" ref-type="bibr">36</xref>), but treatment with weight loss agents such as semaglutide should be considered in patients with schizophrenia and a high risk of CVD, as conventional approaches focusing on lifestyle factors, such as weight-reducing diets and physical activity, have shown limited effects (<xref rid="B37" ref-type="bibr">37</xref>).</p></sec><sec id="s4C"><title>Strengths and Limitations</title><p>Our study has several strengths, including its RCT design and the high rate of completion (91.5%). However, some limitations should be noted. First, our findings may not be generalizable to all patient populations, particularly those without concurrent antipsychotic treatment. Second, although we observed significant metabolic benefits, our sample size may have limited the power to detect smaller, but clinically relevant changes in β-cell function and fasting insulin levels. Third, our study duration was limited to 30 weeks, and longer follow-up may be required to determine changes in these variables. We only used semaglutide 1.0 mg weekly, and it is likely that semaglutide at doses up to 2.4 mg weekly would have shown greater effects. Furthermore, we did not use the gold standard (i.e., the hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp technique) to determine the glucose metabolic condition of our participants but relied on fasting insulin and glucose levels and the corresponding HOMA estimates. However, HOMA estimates have been widely validated as a surrogate marker of insulin resistance, and this method has provided outcomes that correlate well with conventional tests of insulin resistance, such as the hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp (<xref rid="B38" ref-type="bibr">38</xref>). Finally, our data are limited to fasting conditions, as we did not obtain stimulated measures of β-cell function, a clear limitation. Additional data on stimulated HOMA estimates would be valuable to better understand changes before and after semaglutide treatment, especially regarding GLP-1RA–mediated effects on glucose-dependent insulin secretion.</p><p>In conclusion, semaglutide treatment led to significant improvements in glycemic control and insulin sensitivity in the fasting condition, with weight loss appearing to be the primary mediator of these effects. While β-cell function did not change significantly, the observed metabolic benefits support the role of semaglutide as an effective intervention for improving metabolic health in individuals undergoing antipsychotic treatment. Given the high prevalence of insulin resistance and cardiovascular risk in schizophrenia (<xref rid="B39" ref-type="bibr">39</xref>), semaglutide may represent a valuable strategy for mitigating metabolic dysfunction in this at-risk population.</p></sec></sec><sec sec-type="supplementary-material"><p>This article contains supplementary material online at <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://doi.org/10.2337/figshare.31298458" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:title="Link to Semaglutide Effects on Insulin Sensitivity and β-Cell Function in Patients With Schizophrenia, Prediabetes, and Obesity Treated With Second-Generation Antipsychotics: Findings From the HISTORI Trial, a 30-Week Randomized, Place">https://doi.org/10.2337/figshare.31298458</ext-link>.</p></sec></body><back><ack><title>Article Information</title><p><bold>Acknowledgments.</bold> The authors thank Ulla Falkner, clinical research nurse, Research Unit West (Slagelse)–Psychiatry Region Zealand; Birgitte Lundberg, clinical research nurse, Psychiatric Research Unit, Copenhagen University Hospital–Psychiatry Region Zealand; Rikke Skov Jensen, clinical research nurse, Child and Adolescent Psychiatric Research Unit, Psychiatry Region of Southern Denmark; and chemist Lise Pedersen and the Clinical Biochemistry Department, Holbæk Hospital, coordinator for blood sampling in Region Zealand During the preparation of this work, the authors used GPT-4 Turbo to correct grammar, condense text, and enhance academic writing style. <given-names>JM</given-names></string-name></person-group>. <article-title>The origins and drivers of insulin resistance</article-title>. <source>Cell</source>
<year>2013</year>;<volume>152</volume>:<fpage>673</fpage>–<lpage>684</lpage><pub-id pub-id-type="pmid">23415219</pub-id>
